fixes.explanation: Yes, baker. Verse 26 says God sent Moses His servant, and Aaron, whom He had chosen. Then verse 27 says, “They performed His miraculous signs among them, and wonders in the land of Ham.” Moses and Aaron were sent to do what God gave them to do.
That's right. Verse 7 says, “His judgments carry throughout the earth.” Not a corner of the map, the whole earth. And notice the writer says “the LORD our God,” so he counts himself in.

That's what the text says. Verse 13 says, “…they wandered from nation to nation, from one kingdom to another.” Verse 12 calls them few in number, few indeed, and strangers in the land. A small family on the move.

That's right. Verse 14 says, “He rebuked kings on their behalf…” God Himself stepped in for His people. Verse 15 gives His words: “Do not touch My anointed ones! Do no harm to My prophets!” A small family had the biggest backup there is.
Priests aren't named in this verse. Verse 14 says, “He rebuked kings on their behalf…” God was the one doing the rebuking. And the ones He rebuked were kings.
Elders don't show up here. Verse 14 says, “He rebuked kings on their behalf…” The word the writer chose is kings. That's who got rebuked.

Right. Verse 17 says, “He sent a man before them—Joseph, sold as a slave.” Verse 18 adds, “They bruised his feet with shackles and placed his neck in irons,” so this was a hard road. I think this part of the story hurts.

Yes. Verse 19 says Joseph stayed in irons “…until his prediction came true and the word of the LORD proved him right.” The one doing the proving is the word of the LORD. His prediction came true, and that's when the irons stopped.

That's it. Verse 20 says, “The king sent and released him; the ruler of peoples set him free.” Verse 18 had Joseph in irons, so this is a big change from shackles. The king is the one who sent and released him.

Yes, baker. Verse 22 gives the purpose of Joseph's appointment: “to instruct his princes as he pleased and teach his elders wisdom.” Verse 20 had him set free, and verse 21 makes him master of the king's household. That's quite a turn for a man who had been in irons.

Warfare isn't named in this verse. Verse 22 gives the purpose of Joseph's appointment: “to instruct his princes as he pleased and teach his elders wisdom.” Wisdom is the word the writer gives for what the elders would be taught.

Farming isn't named in this verse. The purpose of Joseph's appointment was “to instruct his princes as he pleased and teach his elders wisdom.” Wisdom is the only subject the verse names. I can barely teach my oven to behave, so teaching elders wisdom sounds like a big job.
That's right. Verse 23 says, “Then Israel entered Egypt; Jacob dwelt in the land of Ham.” The psalm uses both names, Israel and Jacob, in that one verse. Egypt is the next stop in the story.

The text goes the other way. Verse 24 says, “…the LORD made His people very fruitful, more numerous than their foes…” Few has turned into very fruitful. The verse says they became more numerous than their foes.
Not in this verse. Verse 23 has Israel entering Egypt, and verse 24 says, “…the LORD made His people very fruitful, more numerous than their foes…” They're in Egypt, and they're growing.

Building store cities isn't in this psalm. Verse 26 says God sent Moses and Aaron, and verse 27 says, “They performed His miraculous signs among them, and wonders in the land of Ham.” Signs and wonders are the work the psalm gives them. The psalm calls them His signs.
That's not what the verse says. Verse 29 says, “He turned their waters to blood and caused their fish to die.” The fish died, and the verse says God caused it. It's a heavy part of the song.

Yes, verse 33 says, “He struck their vines and fig trees and shattered the trees of their country.” Vines, fig trees and the trees of their country all took the hit. It comes right after the hail and lightning of verse 32.

Right. Verse 37 says, “He brought Israel out with silver and gold, and none among His tribes stumbled.” So Israel left with silver and gold. Empty-handed doesn't fit that verse, and neither does a single stumble.

That's not what the text says. Verse 38 says, “Egypt was glad when they departed, for the dread of Israel had fallen on them.” The writer's word is glad. He even gives the reason: the dread of Israel had fallen on them.

That's right. Verse 39 says, “He spread a cloud as a covering and a fire to light up the night.” A covering and a light for the night, both from God's hand. It was a pretty good setup for a desert walk.

Yes, baker. Verse 41 says, “He opened a rock, and water gushed out; it flowed like a river in the desert.” Water gushing out of a rock in the middle of a desert. The verse says it flowed like a river.

A cistern is a fair guess, since it holds water, but the verse doesn't use it. It says, “He opened a rock, and water gushed out; it flowed like a river in the desert.” God opened a rock, and that's where the water gushed from. Rock, not a storage tank.
Yes. Verse 42 says, “For He remembered His holy promise to Abraham His servant.” The writer gives the reason right there. And verse 8 says He remembers His covenant forever.
